strengths: Novel theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.2 rigorously proves block-level factorization reduces NELBO vs. token-wise independence, with formal quantification of the improvement. Theorem 3.3 establishes necessity/sufficiency of soft-conditioning and demonstrates top-k truncation can exclude the global mode.

Well-motivated practical solution: Clearly articulates the coherence problem in parallel DLM sampling and proposes a method that maintains key DLM capabilities (bidirectionality, infilling, self-correction) unlike prior quasi-AR approaches.

Clever soft-conditioning design: Projecting marginals into AR embedding space elegantly bridges DLM's rich information with AR model's representational space. Table 1 ablation convincingly shows soft-conditioning is essential (e.g., 68.9→55.5% accuracy drop with hard-conditioning).

Solid experimental validation on code generation: Comprehensive benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench plus EvalPlus), both static/dynamic parallelism, establishes new Pareto frontier for accuracy vs. latency with 2× speedup maintaining base model accuracy.

Thorough experimental documentation: Detailed experimental setup in Appendix A including tokenizer alignment, special tokens, and extraction logic enables reproducibility. Clear figures effectively illustrate the method.
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: Experiments only on code generation with a single base model (Dream-Coder-7B). Despite the title/abstract suggesting a general DLM method, generalization to other domains, models, and tasks is completely unvalidated. This critically limits impact claims for a method positioned as advancing DLM decoding broadly.

Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.2 predicts larger blocks reduce NELBO (confirmed by Figure 3 training loss), but Figure 4 shows sharp inference degradation at large B (B=8: 29.9% vs B=2: 68.9% on HumanEval). This suggests practical benefits come from the auxiliary AR model rather than block-level diffusion itself, undermining the theoretical motivation.

Artificial generation constraints: Section 3.5 introduces 'candidate scoping' limiting unmasking to 10 blocks to prevent premature EOS prediction. This ad-hoc workaround suggests fundamental instability issues. Table 2 shows extending scope to 50 blocks maintains throughput but drops accuracy significantly, raising questions about the method's robustness.

Incomplete experimental comparisons: No comparison with recent methods (discrete copula diffusion cited but not compared). ADJUST baseline appears weak but comparison unfair given different design goals. No ablation isolating contributions of block-level diffusion vs. auxiliary AR model vs. soft-conditioning alone.

Limited analysis of what the auxiliary model learns: No investigation of which coherence error types are fixed, what the AR model actually learns beyond basic denoising, or how performance varies with vocabulary size and task differences. Soft-conditioning contribution feels somewhat orthogonal to the block-diffusion narrative.

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical importance for DLM deployment
Solid theoretical contributions with rigorous proofs of NELBO improvement (Theorem 3.2) and necessity of full marginals (Theorem 3.3)
Novel soft-conditioning interface elegantly bridges bidirectional DLM and local AR model
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks, generation modes, and non-causal tasks with extensive ablations
Strong empirical results establishing new Pareto frontier: substantial accuracy gains with parallel decoding, 2× speedup with dynamic parallelism, up to 56pp syntax error reduction
Efficient design: 0.6B parameter auxiliary AR model sufficient; larger variants show no consistent improvement
Preservation of DLM capabilities (infilling, planning) demonstrated with non-causal task evaluation
Thorough reproducibility: detailed experimental setup, hyperparameter specifications, and code availability promised
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.3 justifies full marginals but soft-conditioning projection is lossy; no analysis of information loss in embedding projection or guarantees that learned AR recovers target copula
Limited baseline comparisons: only Dream-Coder and ADJUST; missing comparisons to discrete copula diffusion, self-speculative decoding, and other recent methods
Block size fundamental limitation: focus on B≤8 due to sequential AR latency; real code structures may require larger coherent blocks; trade-off under-explored
Batch size 1 latency penalty: 17% throughput reduction (61.4 vs 74.6 tokens/sec) is non-negligible for single-sample inference despite batch 8 amortization
Narrow experimental scope: evaluation restricted to code generation only; no general text, dialogue, or domain generalization assessment
Insufficient statistical rigor: single-seed experiments with no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; difficult to assess robustness
Incomplete AR model analysis: no investigation of what linguistic patterns AR learns, agreement/disagreement with DLM, error propagation, or learning dynamics
Soft-conditioning design choices lack principled justification: expected embedding projection chosen without comparing to alternative projection methods
Limited qualitative analysis: single Figure 1 example of correction; no systematic failure mode analysis, edge case discussion, or error categorization
Unclear generalization: many hyperparameters and strong dependence on specific tokenizers/models; adaptation to other DLM architectures unexplored
